ethiopia.title: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopia's rule of law performance has deteriorated further, with the country ranking 133rd out of 143 countries and jurisdictions in the 2026 World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index, according to the ranking provided for this report. The latest assessment extends a multi-year decline that has seen the country remain near the bottom of global and sub-Saharan African comparisons. The 2026 index, released on 21 October, comes as the WJP warns that authoritarian practices are becoming entrenched worldwide, with weakened checks on executive power, declining judicial independence and restrictions on fundamental freedoms contributing to a prolonged global deterioration in the rule of law. The WJP said the global rule-of-law recession had continued for a ninth consecutive year, with 62% of the countries and jurisdictions assessed recording declines, compared with 38% that improved. Although the share of countries experiencing deterioration fell from 68% in 2025, the overall direction remained negative. The latest findings reinforce concerns about institutional accountability and civic freedoms in Ethiopia, where successive editions of the index have documented persistent weaknesses in constraints on government authority, fundamental rights, open government and the enforcement of regulations. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines A sustained decline across successive editions Ethiopia's latest ranking follows a pattern documented by Addis Standard in previous years. In the 2025 edition, the country ranked 132nd out of 143 countries, with its overall score falling by 2.4% from the previous year to 0.36. It placed 30th among 34 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, highlighting the depth of its institutional weaknesses relative to regional peers. The decline has persisted across multiple editions. Ethiopia ranked 129th out of 142 countries in 2023, with a score of 0.38, after placing 123rd out of 140 countries in 2022. In the 2024 edition, it ranked 130th out of 142 countries, recording a further 2.4% fall in its overall score. The successive declines point to a longer-term deterioration rather than a one-year fluctuation. They also come against a backdrop of armed conflicts, restrictions on civic freedoms and concerns over the independence and effectiveness of public institutions. Checks on government power, fundamental rights remain weak The 2025 index offers a detailed picture of the areas contributing to Ethiopia's poor performance. The country ranked 134th globally for constraints on government powers, 138th for fundamental rights, 135th for open government and 137th for regulatory enforcement. Its rankings were somewhat higher in civil justice, at 124th, and criminal justice, at 104th. It ranked 96th for absence of corruption. The figures suggest that the weakest areas extend beyond the operation of courts. They include the mechanisms through which government decisions are scrutinized, public institutions are held accountable and citizens exercise fundamental freedoms. The WJP's constraints-on-government-powers measure assesses whether those exercising public authority are bound by law and subject to institutional and non-governmental checks. These include legislative oversight, judicial limits on executive authority and the role of an independent press in holding government to account. Ethiopia's low ranking in this category is particularly significant given longstanding concerns about the relationship between political authority and independent institutions. The country's scores in open government and fundamental rights also point to persistent challenges involving access to information, civic participation and freedoms of expression, assembly and association. The index does not, by itself, establish the cause of every institutional weakness or determine responsibility for individual violations. It provides a comparative assessment based on surveys of households and legal practitioners and experts, capturing how the rule of law is experienced and perceived. Authoritarian practices have become entrenched In its 2026 global findings, the WJP identified the expansion of authoritarian practices, the narrowing of civic space and the weakening of checks and balances as the principal forces behind the continuing global decline. "Authoritarianism is no longer merely an emerging trend - it has become entrenched in many parts of the world," Alejandro Ponce, the WJP's executive director, said in the report's accompanying statement. The organization said more than 86% of countries and jurisdictions had experienced sustained five-year declines in at least one of three safeguards against authoritarian rule: constraints on government powers, open government or fundamental rights. The latest assessment also found that freedom of opinion and expression declined in 64% of countries, freedom of assembly and association in 67%, and civic participation in 65%. Judicial limits on government power deteriorated in 63% of countries, while civil justice weakened in 64% and criminal justice in 58%. The WJP said undue executive pressure and government interference were major drivers of institutional deterioration in both civil and criminal justice systems. Although these are global findings rather than Ethiopia-specific figures, they provide context for the challenges reflected in Ethiopia's repeated low rankings. The country's performance in constraints on government power, fundamental rights and open government places those concerns at the center of its rule-of-law record. Conflicts and restrictions on civic space form part of the wider context Ethiopia's ranking comes amid continuing insecurity and serious human rights concerns across several regions. Armed conflicts in Amhara, Oromia and parts of Tigray have contributed to a difficult environment for civilian protection, access to justice and the exercise of basic freedoms. Addis Standard has previously reported on extrajudicial killings, torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearances, as well as restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly. A U.S. State Department assessment of Ethiopia's 2024 human rights record, reported by Addis Standard in August 2025, documented abuses attributed to state and non-state actors in the context of ongoing conflicts. The media environment has also remained under pressure. In March 2026, Addis Standard reported on an assessment by International Media Support documenting continued intimidation, detention and harassment of journalists in Ethiopia. The report recorded at least 44 journalists abducted or detained during 2025, compared with 43 in 2024. Such developments are relevant to the rule-of-law assessment because the index considers not only whether laws exist, but also how effectively institutions protect rights, enforce legal safeguards and constrain the exercise of public power. However, the index's aggregate score does not independently establish a direct causal relationship between any single conflict, detention or restriction and Ethiopia's overall ranking. Rather, its indicators provide a broader framework for assessing institutional performance alongside other documented evidence. Regional position underscores Ethiopia's decline Ethiopia's 2025 position of 30th among 34 sub-Saharan African countries placed it near the bottom of the regional table. Its overall score of 0.36 was substantially below those of regional leaders, including Rwanda, Namibia and Mauritius. The regional picture is itself mixed. The WJP has reported broad deterioration across sub-Saharan Africa, although some countries have recorded improvements in particular years. Ethiopia's continued low placement nevertheless points to the difficulty of reversing the institutional weaknesses identified in successive editions. Globally, the 2026 index covers 143 countries and jurisdictions and draws on more than 215,000 household surveys and 3,400 surveys of legal practitioners and experts. It assesses eight dimensions: constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice. Scores range from zero to one, with higher scores indicating stronger adherence to the rule of law. The annual index is designed to measure how people experience the rule of law in practice, rather than simply whether a country has laws, courts or formal constitutional protections with its findings offering a comparative view of the relationship between legal institutions, public accountability and everyday access to justice. Press Release October 21, 2026 Updated: October 21, 2026 Ethiopian Americans Urge African Union to Include Amhara People and All Major Stakeholders in Ethiopia’s Peace Process October 21, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Congress (SM/file) Washington Update By Mesfin Mekonen Washington, D.C. The Coalition of Ethiopian Americans Civic Organizations has called on the African Union (AU) to ensure that the Amhara people and other major stakeholders are meaningfully included in future peace negotiations aimed at resolving Ethiopia’s ongoing conflicts. In a formal appeal dated October 19, 2026, the coalition urged the AU to pursue a comprehensive, inclusive, and sustainable peace process that addresses the root causes of Ethiopia’s political instability, armed confrontations, and continuing humanitarian crisis. In a letter addressed to His Excellency Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson of the African Union Commission, the coalition emphasized that lasting peace in Ethiopia cannot be achieved without the meaningful participation of all major stakeholders affected by the country’s conflicts. The letter warned that excluding significant political, ethnic, and religious communities risks undermining the legitimacy and long-term success of peace initiatives. The coalition acknowledged the African Union’s leadership in facilitating the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement between the Ethiopian government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). The agreement was an important step toward ending the devastating war in northern Ethiopia. However, the coalition argued that the limited participation of other major stakeholders highlighted the need for a broader approach to peacebuilding across the country. Although the Pretoria Agreement addressed the conflict between its signatories, Ethiopia continues to face armed confrontations, displacement, insecurity, and serious human rights concerns in several regions. According to the coalition, a peace process that addresses only selected parties cannot resolve the wider political grievances, questions of representation, and security concerns affecting Ethiopia’s diverse population. Amhara Community’s Security and Human Rights Concerns The coalition expressed deep concern over reports of killings, forced displacement, attacks on civilians, and other serious human rights violations affecting the Amhara population. It noted that members of the community have raised longstanding concerns about their security, political representation, and treatment within Ethiopia. The letter also highlighted reports of attacks against Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church clergy, worshippers, and religious institutions. Such incidents, the coalition argued, threaten not only human life and property but also religious freedom, cultural heritage, and the social fabric of Ethiopian society. The coalition called for credible and impartial investigations into allegations of serious human rights violations, effective protection for civilians, and accountability for those responsible under applicable law. It also pointed to ongoing armed confrontations involving government forces and various armed groups, including Fano and factions associated with the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), as evidence of the complexity of Ethiopia’s security crisis. The coalition maintained that military action alone cannot resolve the political grievances and security concerns underlying these conflicts. Instead, it urged the African Union to support meaningful dialogue that addresses the root causes of violence and creates a foundation for peaceful coexistence. Seven Recommendations for Sustainable Peace In its appeal to the African Union Commission, the coalition outlined seven recommendations intended to strengthen the prospects for a comprehensive and lasting peace in Ethiopia. First, ensure the meaningful inclusion of the Amhara people. The coalition urged the AU to ensure that representatives capable of articulating the community’s political, security, and human rights concerns participate directly in peace negotiations. Such participation, it stressed, must be substantive rather than symbolic. Second, broaden participation to include all major stakeholders. The coalition called for an inclusive process involving affected communities, political parties, relevant armed actors, civil society organizations, religious institutions, women’s groups, and other stakeholders. It argued that a credible peace process must reflect Ethiopia’s diversity and recognize the legitimate concerns of communities throughout the country. Third, address the root causes of Ethiopia’s conflicts. The coalition urged negotiators to confront longstanding grievances concerning political representation, equality before the law, security, human rights, constitutional governance, and fundamental freedoms. Without addressing these underlying issues, the coalition warned, any agreement risks producing only a temporary cessation of hostilities rather than a durable settlement. Fourth, strengthen civilian protection and religious freedom. The letter called on all parties to protect civilians, prevent attacks on religious institutions, facilitate humanitarian assistance, and respect international human rights and humanitarian law. It also emphasized the need to protect communities facing violence, displacement, and threats to their religious freedom. Fifth, promote impartial investigations and accountability. The coalition called for credible and independent investigations into reported atrocities and serious human rights violations. It urged the African Union to encourage appropriate investigative mechanisms and accountability measures that apply fairly to all parties, regardless of political affiliation or identity. Sixth, support inclusive national dialogue and democratic reform. The coalition emphasized the need for a credible national dialogue that brings Ethiopia’s diverse communities together to address fundamental political disagreements peacefully. Such a process, it argued, should advance constitutional governance, the rule of law, democratic institutions, minority rights, and equal citizenship. Seventh, establish a comprehensive and sustainable peace framework. The coalition encouraged the African Union to work with the Ethiopian government, relevant political and community representatives, and international partners to develop a framework with clear commitments, mechanisms for monitoring implementation, and meaningful opportunities for affected communities to participate in decisions concerning their future. A Call for Stronger African Union Leadership The coalition stressed that Ethiopia’s continuing instability has consequences beyond its national borders, affecting regional security, humanitarian conditions, and stability throughout the Horn of Africa. As a founding member of the Organization of African Unity, the predecessor of the African Union, Ethiopia has historically played an important role in African diplomacy and continental affairs. The coalition argued that the AU has both a responsibility and an opportunity to help the country move away from armed conflict toward peaceful political coexistence. Achieving that objective, the letter emphasized, will require impartial mediation, broad stakeholder participation, respect for human rights, and a willingness to address the legitimate concerns of all affected communities. “There can be no lasting peace in Ethiopia without the meaningful inclusion of the Amhara population and other major stakeholders in the peace process,” the coalition emphasized in its appeal. The letter warned that excluding important communities risks perpetuating the grievances, political divisions, and security challenges that have contributed to Ethiopia’s recurring conflicts. The coalition therefore urged the African Union Commission to make inclusive participation a central principle of its engagement with Ethiopia and to encourage the establishment of a credible peace process that gives all affected communities a meaningful opportunity to shape their country’s future. International Engagement and Accountability In addition to addressing the African Union, the coalition’s letter was copied to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee. The outreach reflects the coalition’s effort to encourage African and international institutions to support a peace process that prioritizes civilian protection, accountability, national reconciliation, and democratic governance. The coalition stated its readiness to support constructive initiatives promoting peace, respect for human rights, and democratic institutions in Ethiopia. It also expressed hope that, under the leadership of the African Union Commission, a more inclusive and impartial process could help address the concerns of Ethiopia’s diverse communities and establish a foundation for lasting stability. Conclusion: Inclusion Is Essential to Lasting Peace Ethiopia’s path toward peace requires more than agreements between selected parties. It requires a process that recognizes the country’s diverse communities, addresses longstanding grievances, protects fundamental rights, and creates meaningful opportunities for political participation. The central message of the Coalition of Ethiopian Americans Civic Organizations is clear: a sustainable peace agreement must include the Amhara people and all other major stakeholders whose participation is necessary to resolve Ethiopia’s interconnected conflicts. For the African Union, the challenge is to help facilitate a peace process that goes beyond ending individual confrontations and addresses the broader political and security issues threatening the country’s future. An inclusive, impartial, and accountable approach would offer a stronger foundation for national reconciliation and peaceful coexistence. Exclusion, by contrast, risks leaving essential grievances unresolved and prolonging the cycle of conflict. As Ethiopia continues to confront serious challenges, the African Union’s leadership will be important in encouraging dialogue, protecting civilians, and supporting a credible political process. Lasting peace will depend on whether all affected communities have a meaningful voice in shaping Ethiopia’s future. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia: UAE carries out reported drone strike against al-Shabab in Puntland Posted by: Horseed Staff The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has carried out its first reported drone strike against al-Shabab militants in northern Somalia in nearly a year, according to security officials cited by AFP. 22 October, 2026 Share Tweet The strike took place on Tuesday at the Galgala mountain pass in Puntland’s Al-Madow mountain range, where the al-Qaeda-linked militant group maintains a presence. The reported attack was the first attributed to the UAE since November 2025. Two local officials told AFP that UAE drones carried out reconnaissance missions on Monday and Tuesday after an explosive device planted by al-Shabab targeted Puntland security forces. The drones, reportedly launched from Bosaso airport, where the UAE maintains a military base, targeted four militants who were allegedly planting roadside bombs, according to the officials. Two of them were wounded. Puntland paramilitary forces subsequently moved into the area and killed the two wounded militants, the officials said. They also said Puntland was expected to announce a new offensive against al-Shabab in the coming days. Somalia has been fighting the Islamist insurgency for nearly two decades. While al-Shabab’s presence in Puntland is considerably smaller than in south-central Somalia, the group has maintained positions in the Al-Madow mountains for years. The UAE is among several foreign countries supporting efforts against al-Shabab. However, its relationship with Somalia’s federal government has deteriorated amid disagreements over Abu Dhabi’s support for regional political actors, particularly in Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991 but has not secured broad international recognition. The reported strike comes amid heightened political tensions in Somalia, with some regional administrations opposing the federal government’s plans for national elections in 2027. The federal government in Mogadishu has not publicly commented on the reported UAE operation. There is also uncertainty over the future of international logistical support for Somalia’s fight against al-Shabab. The United States has announced plans to end funding for a key United Nations logistics operation at the end of 2026. Now, forecasters warn that El Niño flooding in the coming months could push the country’s hardest-hit communities toward famine. 22 October, 2026 Share Tweet New arrivals crowd a Mogadishu displacement camp even as humanitarian services have closed amid funding shortages. Recent forecasts project that the 2026-2027 El Niño season may make the Deyr far more severe, bringing heavy rain and flooding before the end of the year. For families who have spent years watching crops wither and livestock die, more water might sound like relief. It is not. Deyr rain can become torrential, triggering flash floods and causing rivers to overflow. During the 2023 El Niño floods, 1.2 million people were displaced across Somalia. This year, Somalia’s disaster authorities estimate that 2.5 million to 3.5 million people could be exposed to flooding, with as many as 1 million at risk of further displacement. In 2023, forecasts allowed the Somali government, World Food Programme (WFP), and other partners to send early warnings , distribute cash before flooding began, and pre-position supplies in high-risk areas. Similar preparations are underway this year , but much of the network that made that possible no longer exists. The people in the path of the flooding have already lost nearly everything. Years of failed rains killed their livestock and destroyed their harvests, driving many into displacement settlements that sit on low ground near the rivers. Some communities hit by the 2023 floods are still living with destroyed homes, damaged irrigation systems, and lost herds three years later. How flooding makes hunger worse Mother Aisha feeds her 1-year-old daughter Shukri at a CARE-supported health center near Dhahar, Somalia. The health center was forced to close at the end of September 2026. Photo: Sarah Easter/CARE Floodwaters do more than destroy homes. They can wipe out crops and livestock, cut off roads to markets and health facilities, eliminate other sources of income, and force families to leave their homes in search of safety, income, and stability. For people who are eating too little, these losses can quickly deepen hunger. Between October and December, 5.4 million people are projected to face Crisis levels of hunger or worse. Nearly 1.5 million are expected to reach Emergency, when families face severe food shortages or must exhaust the assets they rely on to survive. Around 26,000 displaced people in Baidoa are projected to reach Catastrophe, the highest household classification on the IPC scale. At that point, families still cannot meet their basic food needs even after exhausting extreme ways of coping. People can face starvation, destitution, extremely critical levels of acute malnutrition, and a sharply increased risk of death. Hunger, disease, and fewer services to respond Fadumo, 42, fled violence in Somalia’s Hiiraan region and now lives with her children in a displacement camp outside Mogadishu. Floodwaters can contaminate drinking water, damage toilets and sanitation systems, and increase the risk of diarrhea and other waterborne illnesses. Somalia is already contending with disease outbreaks, including cholera, measles , and diphtheria . For young children, malnutrition and illness can reinforce each other. Malnutrition weakens the body’s ability to fight infection, while illnesses such as diarrhea can make it harder to absorb nutrients, increasing the risk of dehydration. A child who is already experiencing hunger can become much sicker, much faster. Nearly 1.92 million children under five are expected to require treatment for acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027, including 433,000 with severe acute malnutrition. But the services designed to interrupt that cycle are shrinking. Somalia’s humanitarian response relies heavily on funding from governments and other international donors. Since early 2025, humanitarian funding has fallen sharply as major government donors have reduced foreign assistance, with cuts in U.S. funding accounting for a significant part of the decline. Privacy Policy Terms of Service Search Somalia and Uganda Sign Labour Deal to Protect Workers' Rights October 22, 2026 2 min read ZS By Zakaria Soohoyde - Reporter MOGADISHU, 22 October 2026 Somalia and Uganda have signed a bilateral labour agreement aimed at protecting workers’ rights and regulating employment, officials said on Thursday. The agreement was signed by the two countries’ ministries responsible for labour during the Somalia-Uganda Joint Permanent Commission mid-term review, business forum and joint exhibition held in Mogadishu from 20 to 22 October. Uganda’s Labour Minister Henry Tumukunde said the deal was intended to address challenges faced by some Ugandan workers in Somalia, including unpaid wages and employment benefits, the withholding of passports, employment without written contracts and disputes over work permits. In civil aviation, the two governments agreed on a revised text of the Bilateral Air Services Agreement after identifying discrepancies in an earlier version. The revised document will undergo legal review, with signing scheduled for December 2026. The two sides also agreed to sign an agreement on military training and education by 30 December 2026 and establish a joint defence committee. Somalia is expected to nominate its representatives to the committee by 30 October. On economic cooperation, the countries agreed to finalise the establishment of a Joint Permanent Council on Investment and Trade by 30 November. Their investment promotion agencies will also hold regular meetings to assess progress in bilateral cooperation. Related articles Somali Opposition Figures Congratulate Galmudug Leader Despite Disputes Over Election Process Mudavadi: Africa Must Stop Adopting Technology and Start Building Its Own Power Other planned agreements cover health, statistics, customs and product standards, with deadlines established for their completion. The agreed minutes also indicate that some previous commitments remain unfulfilled, including planned business meetings and unresolved challenges affecting Uganda Airlines’ operations in Somalia. The meeting followed the second session of the Joint Permanent Commission held in Kampala on 7-8 October 2025, where the two governments agreed to conduct annual reviews of progress on bilateral commitments. The delegations were led by the permanent secretaries of their respective foreign ministries, Hamza Adan Haadow of Somalia and Vincent Bagiire Waiswa of Uganda. Somalia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdisalam Abdi Ali, formally opened the Mogadishu meeting. Both sides agreed to continue conducting annual reviews of their bilateral agreements and commitments. The third session of the Somalia-Uganda Joint Permanent Commission is scheduled to take place in Somalia in 2027, with the exact date to be determined by the two governments. somalia.content: Why Ilhan Omar’s case gives US Somalis a bad name ARAB NEWS ARAB NEWS GLOBAL ARAB NEWS PK ARAB NEWS FR 23 Oct 2026 Since 1975 SEARCH 検索: × JP ARAB NEWS JP SEARCH 検索: Japan Saudi Arabia Middle East Business Features Arts & Culture × Japan Saudi Arabia Middle East Business Features Arts & Culture JP Home Middle East Why Ilhan Omar’s case gives US Somalis a bad name Why Ilhan Omar’s case gives US Somalis a bad name Short Url: 22 Oct 2026 15:49:27 GMT9 22 Oct 2026 15:49:27 GMT9 Share Accused of immigration fraud and false statements in citizenship documents, the Minnesota congresswoman can face revoking citizenship and deportation Ray Hanania CHICAGO: A federal investigation into how Ilhan Omar, a member of Congress from Minnesota, obtained US citizenship has raised questions about whether she, or her late father, misrepresented her age on immigration documents. If proven, the allegations could expose her to criminal charges, denaturalization and possible deportation. Federal agents searched her Washington home on Oct. 12, just weeks before the midterm elections on Nov. 3, and seized her phone, computers, passport and other documents. The Justice Department has described the search as part of an ongoing criminal investigation but Omar, the US representative for Minnesota’s 5th congressional district since 2019, has not been charged and the government has not publicly disclosed all of its evidence. The focus of the probe is reportedly on whether she or her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, misstated her age on immigration documents. Investigators are examining whether her age was listed as 17, rather than 18, when her father became a US citizen in 2000. This is a key distinction because at the time, minors age 17 or under could be granted citizenship automatically through a parent. Adults, age 18 and over, had to submit an application of their own. Her father’s past in Somalia is also reportedly under scrutiny. Mohamed, a former cab driver and postal worker, died in 2020 from COVID-19 complications. A New York Post report alleged that he “misrepresented himself as a refugee” despite a decades-long military career, including a leadership position under Somali dictator Siad Barre — a claim that, if verified, could have affected his application. The probe also touches on long-running, but unproven, allegations that Omar entered the country illegally, and claims that her previous marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi was arranged to help him obtain immigration benefits, including the suggestion that he is actually her brother. Omar has repeatedly denied the accusations and none of the marriage-related allegations have been established in court. She also faces a separate inquiry into financial disclosures. This centers on two businesses linked to her husband, Tim Mynett, that appeared to leap in value in her 2025 filing. She amended the filings in April this year to greatly reduce the valuations, and her office said the original figures were mistakes that did not properly account for liabilities and ownership. In September, a congressional ethics watchdog recommended clearing her of any wrongdoing, according to reports. CNN described the search of her home this month as “unusually aggressive,” and said it targeted possible false statements on government documents and a potential conspiracy. Before signing off on it, US Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh limited how prosecutors could access materials seized from a sitting lawmaker. The restrictions were intended to protect Omar’s legislative activities, which are shielded from scrutiny by federal prosecutors under the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause. Omar’s attorneys said those safeguards were not followed. In a letter to the Department of Justice, they said agents violated “key restrictions” attached to the warrant, failed to promptly provide her legal team with a copy of the warrant, and did not contact the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel before the search, as required. Citing people familiar with the situation, Politico reported on Tuesday that investigators had not yet accessed Omar’s phone. If they attempt to do so, they must first give her a chance to assert protections on speech or debate, and a court would decide what investigators are allowed to see. Since the raid, investigators have also turned their attention toward Omar’s relatives. Fox News reported on Monday that her sister, author and activist Sahra Noor, “voluntarily” spoke with investigators about Omar’s immigration status. Officials have not confirmed who else was subpoenaed, and Noor did not respond to a request for comment. The evidence made public so far does not establish that Omar knowingly misrepresented information to obtain US citizenship. The Department of Justice has not publicly presented evidence that she knowingly falsified immigration or citizenship documents, and no court has found her guilty of immigration fraud. The DoJ declined to comment when contacted by Arab News. “As a general rule, the department declines to comment on ongoing investigations,” a spokesperson said on Tuesday. Omar previously declined to speak with Arab News and did not respond to another request for comment sent through her campaign website. US law allows the government to seek the revocation of a naturalized citizen’s citizenship if it was obtained illegally, or secured through the concealment of a material fact or willful misrepresentation. To denaturalize Omar, the DoJ would have to bring a civil lawsuit in federal court and prove that she or her father willfully misrepresented a material fact, such as her age, in order to obtain citizenship. If prosecutors brought criminal charges, they could potentially include immigration fraud, false statements on government forms, or conspiracy, depending on the evidence. Any case based solely on statements made during the original naturalization process could face significant time-limit issues, given that Omar became a citizen more than two decades ago. Investigators were reportedly examining whether similar information appeared on later documents, such as passport applications, which could raise separate questions about more recent conduct. If the government successfully revoked Omar’s citizenship, she could face deportation proceedings. Legal experts told CNN that denaturalization was a “relatively rare process” and prosecutors would have to show that any misleading statements were intentional. Between 2008 and June 12, 2026, 166 denaturalization complaints were filed, according to data gathering and research organization the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse. This represents an annual average of fewer than 10 cases, and a minuscule fraction of the hundreds of thousands of people who become naturalized American citizens each year. The investigation has also raised concerns about a possible backlash against the Somali-American community. Jaylani Hussein, executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, described the rhetoric surrounding Omar and the wider Somali community as “Islamophobic, racist, and xenophobic.” In the past, some conservative commentators in Muslim American and Somali American circles have criticized Omar’s progressive positions as inconsistent with the socially conservative and deeply religious values held by many within those communities. In an op-ed published by the Wall Street Journal in 2019, Somali-born author Ayaan Hirsi Ali compared her own experiences with those of Omar, and accused the politician of failing to confront antisemitism within Muslim communities. Omar has rejected the allegations and accused federal authorities of targeting her for political reasons. Her lawyers described the search this month as “vindictive, retributive and politically motivated.” Omar has sought to turn the investigation into a rallying call. In a video posted on Tuesday, she thanked supporters who had sent “$5, $10, $20” and said the contributions would help her fight the administration in Washington. She said the coming period would be “very expensive and challenging” and urged supporters to continue donating. somalia.content: Aid cuts threaten devastating toll in Somalia, ICRC warns - World - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa China-US China-Europe China-Japan China-Africa Home World / Africa Home / World / Africa Aid cuts threaten devastating toll in Somalia, ICRC warns By VICTOR RABALLA in Nairobi, Kenya | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-10-22 21:27 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE A sharp decline in humanitarian funding could have devastating consequences for vulnerable communities in Somalia as looming floods compound the effects of drought and conflict. The head of the International Committee of the Red Cross in the country has warned that the beginning of the El Nino in some parts of the country risks deaths and property damage if urgent measures are not taken. Antoine Grand made an appeal to international donors to sustain assistance to the Horn of Africa nation, saying the closure of nutrition centers and health facilities was leaving families with fewer places to turn as successive crises exhausted their ability to recover. "We know there are other priorities in the world today, but don't forget about Somalia," Grand said. He estimated that humanitarian funding for Somalia had fallen from about $2.3 billion in 2022 to roughly $300-$350 million, leaving a response already focused on the most urgent needs severely underfunded. Aid organizations had prioritized essential, lifesaving activities, yet the United Nations humanitarian appeal was only about 30 percent funded, he said. "When you reduce that aid drastically, then it is brutal and people suffer," Grand said. The UN and its partners launched an $852 million appeal in January to assist 2.4 million people in Somalia this year. Grand said funding shortages across the humanitarian sector had forced nutrition centers to close, reduced support for hospitals and halted water and resilience projects. "At clinics supported by the ICRC and the Somali Red Crescent Society, patient numbers had nearly doubled as surrounding facilities closed," he said. The impact was especially severe for malnourished children, as access to treatment continue to dwindle. Somalia's vulnerability stems from the combination of prolonged conflict, repeated climate shocks and weak public services, he said. Around 3.3 million people are displaced, with many living in settlements where access to clean water, sanitation and healthcare is limited. Families that lose livestock or crops during drought have little opportunity to rebuild before another emergency strikes. "More and more Somali families are really on the brink of just collapsing," Grand said. He said the impending floods could deepen losses, particularly along the Shabelle and Juba rivers. In a warning issued last week, the ICRC said anticipated El Nino conditions could intensify the October-December rains, threatening farmland and displacement settlements. Grand described the dilemma facing farmers near Jowhar, where planting risks losing scarce seeds to floodwaters, while leaving fields idle would deepen food insecurity and hunger. He said early warnings are helping families move before flooding, giving them time to take livestock, household belongings and important documents. ICRC and Somali Red Crescent have stocked supported health facilities with additional medicines, positioned emergency supplies near vulnerable communities and prepared boats for rescue operations and aid deliveries. "Teams have also protected 38 strategic water points to reduce the risk of floodwater contamination and waterborne disease," Grand added. Beyond emergency assistance, he called for sustained investment in reliable water systems, roads, drainage and flood protection to help communities withstand future shocks. "Anticipatory action, preparedness, resilience is extremely important. We need to invest in that. The more we invest in preparing for the next crisis, the less impact will this next crisis have," Grand said. somalia.content: Somali Media Officials Begin 21-Day AI and Counter-Disinformation Training in China - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Technology & Innovation Nationwide Somali Media Officials Begin 21-Day AI and Counter-Disinformation Training in China October 22, 2026 5 min read JINHUA , A 21-day training programme for 27 officials from Somalia’s Ministry of Information, Culture and Tourism has opened in Jinhua, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, focusing on modern media strategies, artificial intelligence, and combating misinformation. The programme, delivered by experts from Zhejiang Normal University, brings together directors, heads of government media departments, and other ministry personnel. Participants will study modern media strategies, the application of AI in communication, media management, and techniques for identifying and countering false information. The initiative is part of broader efforts to strengthen the professional skills of Somali government media staff as the country seeks to modernise its public communication systems and adapt to changes in the digital media landscape. A Relationship Built Over Months of Engagement The training did not emerge in isolation. It follows a series of high-level engagements between Mogadishu and Beijing on media and technology cooperation throughout 2026. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Somalia’s AI integration , the Ministry of Information has already implemented advanced AI systems in national media operations, including automated translation, content generation, and digital distribution algorithms that have reduced editorial production time. In August 2026, Information Minister Abdulfatah Kasim Mohamud met with Cao Shumin, Minister of China’s National Radio and Television Administration, in Beijing to discuss media modernisation, institutional capacity building, and professional training. The Minister also participated in the China-Africa Media Cooperation Forum, where he called for stronger support to modernise Somali broadcasting infrastructure, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Somalia’s engagement with Chinese and Arab media institutions . At the opening ceremony in Jinhua, Zhu Yifeng, Vice-President of Zhejiang Normal University, said the workshop would promote the exchange of media expertise, strengthen bilateral ties, and advance cooperation between Somalia and China. Abdishakur Ali Ahmed, Director of the Media Strategy Department at Somalia’s Ministry of Information, said the training offered government media representatives an opportunity to learn from China’s experience in modernising its media sector. He thanked the Chinese government, organisers, and institutions involved, particularly the Chinese Ministry of Commerce, which financed the training, and the Chinese Embassy in Somalia, led by Ambassador Wang Yu, which facilitated the initiative. The Strategic Logic and Its Limits China’s engagement with Somali media is part of a broader pattern of Beijing’s involvement in Africa’s information and communication sectors, alongside its expanding economic and security ties with Mogadishu. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of China’s trade policy , Beijing has extended zero-tariff access to all 53 African nations, and the two countries have deepened defence and security cooperation. The media training represents another dimension of a relationship that now spans trade, security, and information. For Somalia, the appeal is practical. The country’s state media infrastructure remains weak, despite recent investments. In 2025, the Ministry of Information established Somalia’s first Media Satellite Teleport in over three decades, a facility intended to modernise broadcasting capabilities, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the teleport launch . But infrastructure alone is insufficient. The government has struggled to counter Al-Shabaab ’s sophisticated propaganda operations and to manage the rapid spread of misinformation during political crises. The challenges facing Somali media are not limited to technical capacity. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of media freedom concerns , independent outlets have accused the government of orchestrating digital censorship campaigns, including copyright strikes and bot-driven harassment against critical reporting. Journalists have been arrested and assaulted by security forces, with press freedom organizations documenting a pattern of intimidation. Critical Note The Jinhua training programme is a welcome investment in Somali media capacity, and the focus on artificial intelligence and counter-disinformation addresses genuine gaps in the government’s communication apparatus. The involvement of the Chinese Ministry of Commerce as a financier and the embassy in Mogadishu as a facilitator indicates a level of institutional commitment that suggests this is not a one-off gesture. But the programme also raises questions that its organisers have not addressed. AI tools and modern media strategies are only as effective as the institutions that deploy them. Somalia’s Ministry of Information has struggled with limited budgets, political interference, and a state media apparatus that many Somalis view with skepticism. A 21-day training course can introduce new techniques, but it cannot resolve these structural weaknesses. The deeper concern is one of orientation. China’s model of media management involves tight state control over information flows, a framework that is fundamentally different from the pluralistic, if chaotic, media environment that has emerged in Mogadishu over the past decade. The training is framed as technical, but the techniques being transferred are not politically neutral. How Somalia’s government media officials apply what they learn in Jinhua will depend on the political culture they return to. The programme can teach them how to use AI to detect misinformation. It cannot teach them how to resist the temptation to use the same tools for political advantage. The same ministry that is sending officials to learn about countering disinformation is the one accused of orchestrating digital censorship at home . CAF ضغوط على الكبار بعد جولة ذهاب مثيرة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا "توتال إنرجيز" CAF نشرت: الثلاثاء, 20 أكتوبر 2026 تواجه بعض أكبر الأندية الأفريقية تحدياً صعباً للحفاظ على طموحاتها القارية، وذلك في أعقاب جولة مليئة بالمفاجآت ضمن منافسات دوري أبطال أفريقيا (TotalEnergies CAF) لموسم 2026/2027. فقد تعادل حامل اللقب "ماميلودي صنداونز"، بينما تلقى "الترجي" -الفائز باللقب أربع مرات- هزيمة مفاجئة، وذلك قبل خوض مباريات الإياب الحاسمة في الدور التمهيدي الثاني . وحقق نادي "السويحلي" الليبي مفاجأة مدوية بفوزه على "الترجي" بنتيجة 1-0، كما تغلب "رينجرز إنترناشيونال" النيجيري على "مولودية الجزائر" بنتيجة 2-0، وبالنتيجة ذاتها تفوق "سكوتلاند إف سي" الزيمبابوي على العملاق الأنغولي "بترو أتلتيكو"؛ وهي نتائج قلبت موازين المنافسة على التأهل لدور المجموعات . وفي الوقت الذي نجحت فيه أندية مثل "يانغ أفريكانز" التنزاني، و"نهضة بركان" المغربي، و"الهلال" السوداني في تحقيق أفضليات مريحة، تواجه أندية كبرى أخرى مهاماً صعبة في مباريات الإياب المقررة في الفترة ما بين 23 و25 أكتوبر . أُقيمت 15 مباراة ضمن جولة الذهاب خلال عطلة نهاية الأسبوع، بينما ستُجرى المباراة المتبقية بين "15 دي أغوستو" من غينيا الاستوائية و"سيمبا" التنزاني يوم الأربعاء . ويتأهل الفائزون الـ 16 من مواجهات الدور التمهيدي الثاني إلى دور المجموعات، الذي من المقرر أن ينطلق في أواخر شهر نوفمبر . ومن أبرز مفاجآت الجولة ما حدث في مدينة مصراتة، حيث فاز "السويحلي" الليبي على "الترجي" التونسي بنتيجة 1-0، مما يضع العملاق التونسي أمام ضرورة تقديم أداء قوي في مباراة الإياب على أرضه لتجنب الخروج المبكر من البطولة . كما يواجه حامل اللقب "ماميلودي صنداونز" مباراة إياب مصيرية، بعد تعادله سلبياً (0-0) أمام "ويليتي" الأنغولي في مدينة لوبانغو . وفي المقابل، حقق "رينجرز إنترناشيونال" النيجيري واحدة من أبرز نتائج جولة الذهاب بفوزه على "مولودية الجزائر" بنتيجة 2-0 في مدينة أبيوكوتا . كما تصدر "سكوتلاند إف سي" الزيمبابوي المشهد بفوزه على أرضه بنتيجة 2-0 على "بترو أتلتيكو" الأنغولي، بفضل هدفين سجلهما اللاعبان الدوليان السابقان "خاما بيليات" و"نوليدج موسونا"، ليمنحا فريقهما انتصاراً ثميناً. وحقق فريق "يانغ أفريكانز" التنزاني أكبر فوز خارج أرضه في هذه الجولة، بتغلبه على "سي إف إف إيه " (CFFA) من مدغشقر بنتيجة 4-0، كما استهل فريق "نهضة بركان" المغربي مشواره بنجاح بفوزه خارج دياره على "ستار سبورت أكاديمي" من سيراليون بنتيجة 2-0 . وعاد فريق "الهلال" السوداني من إثيوبيا بفوز ثمين بنتيجة 2-0 على حساب "بن سيداما "، بينما تألق فريق "كولومب سبورتيف" الكاميروني خارج ملعبه أيضاً، محققاً الفوز على "تينغيث" السنغالي بنتيجة 2-0 في داكار . وتسعى هذه الأندية الأربعة الآن للحفاظ على تفوقها وضمان التأهل إلى دور المجموعات . كما حقق كل من "الزمالك" و"بيراميدز" المصريين الفوز خارج أرضهما بنتيجة 1-0، مما عزز فرصهما في التأهل، في حين انتزع "أورلاندو بايرتس" الجنوب أفريقي فوزاً ثميناً خارج ملعبه على "أفريكان ستارز" الناميبي بنتيجة 1-0 . وتأمل هذه الأندية الثلاثة في استغلال ميزة اللعب على أرضها في مباريات الإياب الحاسمة . من جانبه، يواجه فريق "تي ​​بي مازيمبي" -الفائز باللقب الأفريقي خمس مرات- رحلة صعبة إلى تونس، بعد تعادله بنتيجة 1-1 على أرضه في لوبومباشي أمام "النادي الأفريقي" التونسي . كما حقق "أسيك ميموزا" الإيفواري تعادلاً ثميناً بنتيجة 1-1 خارج ملعبه أمام "المغرب الفاسي". وفي مواجهة أخرى اتسمت بالندية، تغلب "إف سي سان بيدرو" الإيفواري على "إف سي نواذيبو" الموريتاني بنتيجة 2-1، مما يجعل حظوظ الفريقين قائمة في مباراة الإياب بموريتانيا . أما فريق "هورويا" الغيني، فسيسافر لمواجهة "المريخ" السوداني وهو يحمل في جعبته تقدماً ضئيلاً بنتيجة 1-0، بعد فوزه في كوناكري . ونظراً لأن فارق هدف واحد فقط يفصل بين الفريقين، فإن مباراة الإياب تعد بمواجهة أخرى قوية ومحتدمة . وضعت النتائج المسجلة في مختلف أنحاء القارة عدداً من الأندية العريقة أمام خطر الإقصاء المبكر، في حين باتت فرق أخرى طموحة على أعتاب التأهل إلى دور المجموعات. مع اقتراب مباريات الإياب الحاسمة، تستعد المنافسة لعطلة نهاية أسبوع أخرى مليئة بالمواجهات الحاسمة حيث تسعى الأندية المتبقية إلى حجز مكان لها في دور الـ16 في أفريقيا . دوري أبطال أفريقيا توتال انرجيز الأزرق تبرير رئيس الاتحاد، الذي أرجع الهزيمة إلى تأخر انضمام لاعبي الفريق إلى معسكر "صقور الجديان"، نتيجة ارتباطهم بمباراة ودية أمام أهلي طرابلس الليبي، مما أربك ترتيبات سفرهم. إدارة الهلال السوداني تستنكر تصريحات سر الختم من جانبه، وصف رامي كمال، عضو مجلس إدارة الهلال السوداني تصريحات رئيس الاتحاد بأنها "جانبت الصواب" وتعد محاولة للهروب من المسؤولية، وشدد كمال على رفض النادي إقحامه في نتائج المنتخب، مؤكدًا أنّ الهلال ظل داعمًا للاتحاد السوداني انطلاقًا من مسؤوليته الوطنية وحرصه على مصلحة الكرة السودانية. كما دعا كمال إلى ضرورة تقييم نتائج المنتخب بناءً على أسس فنية وإدارية موضوعية، بعيدًا عن تحميل الأطراف الأخرى المسؤولية، أو إطلاق تصريحات قد تضر باستقرار المنظومة الكروية في البلاد. اقرأ أيضًا الهلال السوداني يصنع الحدث و"غربال" على موعد مع المجد اتحاد الكرة يحسم مستقبل مدرب منتخب السودان كواسي أبياه وأكد إداري الهلال السوداني إدراك الجميع للظروف الاستثنائية التي تعمل في ظلها منظومة كرة القدم السودانية، مشيرًا إلى أن ناديه جزء أصيل من هذه المنظومة، وأن مجلس إدارته يعمل بجد مع شركائه، وفي مقدمتهم الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم وبقية الأندية، لتجاوز التحديات الراهنة وضمان استمرارية النشاط الرياضي وتطويره. كما شدد على أنّ المرحلة الحالية تتطلب من جميع الأطراف التحلي بروح المسؤولية المشتركة، وتعزيز الحوار والتنسيق، والمشاركة الفاعلة في اتخاذ القرارات الاستراتيجية التي تخدم الكرة السودانية وتدفع بمسيرتها نحو الاستقرار، بدلًا من تبادل الاتهامات عبر وسائل الإعلام. واختتم بالتأكيد على أنّ رفضهم لتصريح رئيس الاتحاد لا يعني إنكار الجهود الإيجابية التي يبذلها الدكتور معتصم جعفر وأعضاء مجلس إدارته في دعم الأندية المشاركة في البطولات الأفريقية باسم السودان، مؤكدًا على أنّ football.summary: الهلال السوداني رد على تصريحات رئيس اتحاد الكرة السوداني، الذي انتقد أداء الفريق في الدوري. جاء الرد من إدارة الهلال عبر بيان رسمي، حيث أكدت أن الانتقادات غير مبررة وأن الفريق يسعى لتحقيق النجاح رغم التحديات. كما أشار الهلال إلى التزامه بتطوير كرة القدم في السودان ودعم اللاعبين. البيان شدد على أهمية التعاون بين الأندية والاتحاد لتحقيق الأهداف المشتركة، ودعا إلى التركيز على تحسين الأداء بدلاً من الانشغال بالتصريحات. هذه الحرب الكلامية تعكس التوترات الحالية في الساحة الرياضية السودانية، حيث يسعى كل طرف لتأكيد موقفه.
